questions.question: A statBar is a straight bar cut into 8 equal squares. Each square stands for 5 books. Exactly 4 of the squares are shaded. How many books does the shaded part stand for?
questions.explain: Each shaded square stands for 5 books, so 4 shaded squares mean 4 x 5 = 20 books. The most common trap is counting the squares themselves and answering 4, which forgets that one square stands for 5.

questions.question: A statBar is cut into 10 equal squares. All 10 squares together stand for 50 stickers, and every square stands for the same amount. What does ONE square stand for?
questions.explain: The whole bar of 50 stickers is shared equally by 10 squares, so one square stands for 50 divided by 10 = 5 stickers. The trap is assuming one square always means 1 sticker, which is one-to-one, not many-to-one.

questions.question: A statBar is cut into 6 equal squares. Each full square stands for 5 kg of recycling. The shaded part is 3 full squares and 1 half square. How many kilograms does the shaded part stand for?
questions.explain: Three full squares are 3 x 5 = 15 kg, and a half square is half of 5, which is 2.5 kg, so the total is 17.5 kg. Children often drop the half square or count it as a whole one instead of taking half of the scale.

questions.question: A statBar is cut into equal squares and 7 of them are shaded. Each square stands for 5 minutes of reading. Ben says the bar shows 7 minutes. Which sentence best explains what is going on?
options: Ben is right, because 7 squares are shaded.
Ben should count each square as half of 5, so the bar shows 17.5 minutes.
Ben should have added 5 and 7, so the bar shows 12 minutes.
Ben read each square as 1 minute, but each square stands for 5 minutes, so the bar shows 35 minutes.
questions.explain: With a many-to-one scale, the number of squares is not the answer; you must trade each square for what it stands for, so 7 x 5 = 35 minutes. The classic mistake is reading a scale of 5 as if it were 1.

questions.question: On a library pictograph, one star stands for 5 books. Division 4 has 6 stars and Division 5 has 4 stars. How many MORE books did Division 4 borrow than Division 5?
questions.explain: Change the stars into books first: 6 x 5 = 30 and 4 x 5 = 20, so the difference is 10 books. Comparing stars instead of books gives 2, which ignores that each star stands for 5.

questions.question: A Grade 4 class counted the water bottles recycled by four divisions: 45, 30, 25 and 50. They decide to draw a pictograph where one bottle symbol stands for 5 bottles. Which sentence best explains why that scale is a good choice?
options: Because a scale of 5 makes the real counts smaller, so 50 bottles becomes 10 bottles.
Because every count is a multiple of 5, so the class draws at most 10 symbols instead of 50.
Because each symbol still stands for 1 bottle, it is just drawn 5 times bigger.
Because a scale of 5 means half symbols are never allowed on a pictograph.
questions.explain: A many-to-one scale changes how many symbols you draw, not how many bottles there really are, and a scale of 5 fits data made of multiples of 5. The trap is thinking the scale shrinks the real amounts.

questions.question: On a cycling pictograph, one full symbol stands for 5 km. Maya's row has 5 full symbols. Ravi's row has 3 full symbols and 1 half symbol. How much farther did Maya cycle than Ravi?
questions.explain: Maya cycled 5 x 5 = 25 km and Ravi cycled 15 km plus half of 5, which is 2.5 km, so Ravi cycled 17.5 km and the gap is 7.5 km. Ignoring Ravi's half symbol, or counting it as a full one, is the usual slip.

questions.question: On a bar graph of favourite winter sports, the numbers up the side are labelled 0, 5, 10, 15, 20 and so on, so every mark is worth the same amount. The hockey bar ends exactly 7 marks above 0. How many students chose hockey?
questions.explain: Each mark on the side stands for 5 students, so 7 marks mean 7 x 5 = 35 students. Reading the bar as 7 treats a scale of 5 like a scale of 1.

questions.question: Aiden made a pictograph where one book symbol stands for 1 book, and he drew 20 symbols for the Grade 3 class. Priya redraws the very same data, but on her pictograph one book symbol stands for 5 books. How many symbols will Priya draw for the Grade 3 class?
questions.explain: The class still has 20 books, and since each of Priya's symbols carries 5 books, she needs 20 divided by 5 = 4 symbols. A bigger scale means fewer symbols for the same amount, so drawing 20 again or multiplying by 5 misses what the scale does.

questions.question: A Burnaby class tracked juice recycled, and one carton symbol stands for 5 L. Monday has 2 full symbols, Tuesday has 3 full symbols and 1 half symbol, and Wednesday has 1 full symbol and 1 half symbol. How many litres were recycled in the three days altogether?
questions.explain: Monday is 10 L, Tuesday is 15 + 2.5 = 17.5 L and Wednesday is 5 + 2.5 = 7.5 L, giving 35 L in total. Each half symbol is half of the scale, so it is worth 2.5 L, not 0 L and not a full 5 L.

questions.question: Two classes made pictographs of the cans they collected. The Grade 4 graph uses one can symbol for 5 cans and shows 5 symbols. The Grade 5 graph uses one can symbol for 1 can and shows 20 symbols. Which class collected more cans, and why?
options: Grade 5, because 20 symbols is more than 5 symbols.
They collected the same number, because graphs with different scales cannot be compared.
Grade 4, because 5 symbols stand for 5 x 5 = 25 cans, and 25 is more than 20.
Grade 5, because one symbol always stands for one can.
questions.explain: Before comparing, change each row into real cans using its own scale: Grade 4 has 25 cans and Grade 5 has 20 cans. The big trap is comparing how many symbols you see instead of what those symbols stand for.

questions.question: A Kamloops class recycled 30 kg of paper in week 1 and 15 kg in week 2. They will show the two-week total in one row of a pictograph, where one bin symbol stands for 10 kg. How many symbols should the row have?
questions.explain: Find the total first, 30 + 15 = 45 kg, then trade it for symbols: 45 divided by 10 = 4 full symbols with 5 kg left over, and 5 kg is half of 10, so it needs 1 half symbol. Drawing 45 symbols treats the scale as one-to-one, and 4 or 5 full symbols either drops the leftover 5 kg or wrongly grows it into a full symbol.
